atoms.b: More and more ((++soldiers emperors)) were recalled from Roman Britain, leaving fewer behind to guard the ((++forts palaces)). As raids continued, life on the frontier became harder for those who remained.

Rome could also no longer afford to pay or ((++feed feat)) its soldiers properly. There wasn’t enough ((++gold euro)) and silver, so coins were mixed with cheaper metals. This meant that each coin was worth less.

instruction.text: Read the letter and answer the question.

b: ++The Roman army is not providing him enough food.
It is difficult to farm olives in Britain.
The local Britons are eating all his food.
++He noticed that the soldiers are being paid less.
There are not enough free-time activities.
++There are fewer soldiers and more raids.
They don’t like the weather in Britain.
Life in Britain is too boring.

feedback.finish: After years in Britain, many Roman soldiers were frustrated. Underfed and underpaid, they were ready to go home.

trainers.instruction: Read the text and answer the questions.

atoms.text: As the number of raids escalated, Britons also became increasingly unhappy with their quality of life under Roman rule. Many had money and valuables stolen and feared for their safety.
With violence on the roads, traders also became more afraid to travel to Roman Britain. This meant that wealthy Britons could no longer buy the luxuries they were used to.

atoms.a: In which two ways did increasing raids make life harder for Britons?
b: Britons were paid more by the Romans.
++Britons could not buy the products they wanted.

atoms.a: Why were fewer goods reaching Roman Britain?

trainers.instruction: Look at this archaeological dig site and select the correct items.

feedback.finish: Roman coins and other valuables have been found purposely buried together in Bath.

trainers.instruction: Listen and select the correct answer.

atoms.a: Why do you think people were burying their valuables?

b.sound: They were afraid of being robbed by raiders.
They didn’t have enough room in their homes.

trainers.instruction: Fill in the gaps in this conversation between two Britons.

atoms.b: It’s good to see you, Catell. How have your family been handling the ((++raids summer))?
It’s been difficult. I’ve buried all my ((++coins clothes)) near my home so that the Scots cannot find them.
That’s a good idea. My village had ((++Picts Pikes)) come through just last week, and the Romans were nowhere to be seen!
What an outrage! With all these Roman ((++forts courts)), you’d think they could protect us!

feedback.finish: By this time, Britain had been part of the Roman Empire for over 300 years. Many Britons had accepted Roman rule and expected the empire to defend them.
